title: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In large genera the amount of difference between species is often exceedingly small, so that their species resemble varieties more than do species of small genera.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Now Fries has remarked in regard to plants, and Westwood in regard to insects, that in large genera the amount of difference between the species is often exceedingly small. I have endeavoured to test this numerically by averages, and, as far as my imperfect results go, they always confirm the view.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges”. Scope: plant and insect genera

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-11: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Sequence databases provide millions of comparable species distances and taxonomies provide genus sizes. The predicted contrast can be tested quickly and robustly across clades.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare standardized pairwise genetic and morphological distances among species in large versus small genera, with phylogenetic age and sampling controls. Smaller within-genus distances in large genera support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Morphological coverage is uneven.

Large genera may be younger or taxonomically oversplit.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.81
analysis feasibility: 0.84
data existence: 0.93
data adequacy: 0.78
operationalizability: 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Pairwise distances and genus sizes are both in open trees, barcode libraries, and, more patchily, trait tables. A negative relationship is directly computable for insects and many plant genera. Because small gaps are partly how large genera get delimited, morphology is the less circular measure and it is the less complete dataset, so the test remains only partly discriminating.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress mean pairwise morphological or genetic distance among congeners on genus richness. Smaller distances in larger genera would support the pattern; equal or larger distances would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Taxonomists split large genera more finely, which shrinks genetic distances by practice.

Trait databases often store one mean per species and miss the characters Darwin compared.

Phylogenetic distance and morphological difference can disagree about which genera are 'close'.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.5
operationalizability: 0.78
analysis feasibility: 0.62
